Hi Jo,

Could you let me know when the shelf brackets are expected? We hope to open the shared craft cupboard on Tuesday, provided they arrive by Monday afternoon.

The cupboard is beside the north window. Blue labels mark tools, which only workshop members can borrow. White labels mark paper, which anyone attending an open session can use in the room. Both are free.

Thanks for helping us get it ready!

Mina

Hi Eli,

Thanks for offering to bring the folding chairs. We need six for Saturday; if you can bring only four, that is fine too. Please leave them inside the side entrance.

Best,
Ruth

I tried a borrowed shallow tray for the stamp pads during two club sessions. The pads were easier to find, which was encouraging, although we also had fewer people than usual. I suspect the tray helped; I cannot quite separate its contribution from that of a quieter room. Apparently a place to put things counts as an innovation. Before buying trays for every group, I would like to try it again with a full table and see whether the innovation survives the company.
I prefer a small trial before we buy more trays. The first session looked promising, but the room was unusually quiet. That is an observation, not yet a result.

Green cards reserve workshop places; orange cards put people on the waiting list. Both need a name and contact number. Collect them at afternoon’s end, after packing away boxes and samples. Collecting an orange card does not reserve a place: someone must cancel, and the organizer must confirm the replacement by phone. Green-card holders need no extra call.

You can take lantern kits home after the afternoon session, including the smaller sample lantern beside the large demonstration kit. The demonstration kit must stay on the long table. Return kits to the grey basket by noon the following Friday. If you cannot return yours by then, tell Noor before taking it home.

Another three-week trial seems reasonable, but June’s figures do not establish demand in October. Log A recorded 14, 9, and 16 entries between 6 and 7 p.m. on three Thursdays; repeat entries could include the same person, so we do not know how many unique visitors attended. Memo B says the experiment ran only in June, when two local classes were running. Visitors were not asked about the classes, so their effect on attendance is unknown. The October trial is proposed, not approved. If it goes ahead, counting unique visitors and asking about class attendance would help clarify the results.
The desk recorded eight exchanges on the first Saturday and eleven on the second. Rain on the first day may be relevant, but these notes do not tell us whether it affected attendance.

Ada propped the biscuit tin lid against a spool of thread and stepped back from the kitchen table. Her painted moon shone over the shoebox theatre, its chipped edge plainly visible.

Basil arrived carrying a paper dragon.

“Excellent shield,” he said. “The knight will be relieved.”

“It’s the moon, Uncle Basil.”

“Even better. A shield with a night job.”

Ada turned the lid until the chipped edge faced the audience. She had painted around it, and refused to let Basil cover it with a cloud.

“It gives the sky some character,” she said.

In Little Tupp, where the play was due to open after tea, character was plentiful and spare biscuit tins were scarce.

Basil lowered the dragon through the top of the shoebox. Its head caught on the curtain.

Ada held the moon steady while her uncle trimmed the dragon’s left ear.

I tried to concentrate on the mountain, which leaned noticeably towards the cheap seats. The box made an excellent brace, though I suspected this was not why Leo had entrusted it to me. I turned it carefully, keeping its single lock away from a patch of wet glue. Something inside shifted with a small, ordinary clink. I imagined introducing myself to Vera on Sunday by apologizing for having used her mystery as scenery. Then I cut a strip of cardboard, folded it into a support, and slid the box clear.
